**John Michael McCarthy** (born October 12, 1962) is a retired American mixed martial arts (MMA) referee best known for officiating numerous bouts promoted by the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), dating back to UFC 2.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCarthy_(referee)#cite_note-tapology-1) He is credited as being one of the greatest and most recognizable referees in combat sports history and an important figure in the mixed martial arts world, helping create the Unified Rules of MMA after initially creating the original rule book of the UFC. He currently is a commentator for the Professional Fighters League (PFL) and co-hosts the combat sports-based podcast "Weighing In" with former fighter Josh Thomson.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCarthy_(referee)#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCarthy_(referee)#cite_note-3)
McCarthy spent some time as an officer of the Los Angeles Police Department, retiring around 2008.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCarthy_(referee)#cite_note-:0-4)
In 1993, he became involved with the newly created Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) fighting tournament. He was the referee for UFC 2, launching a career as a UFC referee. The UFC initially started with very few rules, but McCarthy gave feedback that it was too dangerous and suggested additional rules, many of which were adopted. Saying the catch phrase originally coined by boxing referee Mills Lane, McCarthy would often start matches by saying "let's get it on" to the fighters, which became an iconic catchphrase that is associated with him and his refereeing.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCarthy_(referee)#cite_note-:0-4)

The nickname of "Big John" came about because of his size and stature. He stands 6 ft 3 in (1.91 m) and weighs 265 lb (120 kg); making him larger than the majority of the athletes over whom he presides. According to a UFC interview, the nickname was given to him by UFC co-founder and promoter Art Davie. McCarthy recalls that the nickname began when he forcibly lifted Davie off the ground and held him in the air.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCarthy_(referee)#cite_note-5)
In 2018, McCarthy retired from UFC refereeing, and moved to Bellator as a commentator.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCarthy_(referee)#cite_note-6) He currently serves as a judging and rules analyst for the Professional Fighters League (PFL), who acquired Bellator in 2023.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCarthy_(referee)#cite_note-7)

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
October 22, 2026
When the cage door closes, two fighters and one referee are left inside. For more than 15 years, that referee has often been Marc Goddard.
Born in Birmingham, Goddard has officiated UFC world title fights before 60,000 fans. He has refereed nearly 2,000 bouts worldwide. Fighters, coaches and fans count him among the most respected officials in mixed martial arts.
> “The responsibility I carry as a referee is paramount.”
Here’s how a former West Midlands fighter became one of the UFC’s most trusted referees.

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## Who Is Marc Goddard?
Marc Goddard is an English MMA referee from Birmingham. He has refereed in the UFC since 2008. Before refereeing, he was a professional fighter, coach and promoter, so he’s seen the sport from every side of the cage.
Away from fight night, Goddard is Director of Regulatory Affairs at the International Mixed Martial Arts Federation (IMMAF). He also helped found the UK safety charity Safe MMA. In 2022, he was named Referee of the Year at the Fighters Only World MMA Awards.

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## How Did Marc Goddard Become an MMA Referee?
Goddard came to refereeing as a fighter. He competed as a heavyweight in the early days of the British MMA scene, finishing with a reported professional record of 7-6-1.
He got his first refereeing job by accident in 2004. A promoter’s referee didn’t show up, and Goddard stepped in. He kept fighting at the same time, and that gave him a view from both sides.
> “When I first started reffing in 2004, I was still competing. I was still fighting. So I kind of understood from that side of it.”
He learned early how seriously to take the job. Goddard has also coached fighters, including the young Leon Edwards. He still trains himself.
> “Still, being a martial artist is very important to me. From a personal point of view, I’ll never stop.”

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## When Did Marc Goddard Start Refereeing in the UFC?
Goddard made his UFC debut at UFC 89 in his home city of Birmingham in 2008. Lightweight Jim Miller made his UFC debut on the same card. Goddard later marked the anniversary on social media: “We both made our debuts for the organization that night!”
Since then, he has refereed UFC events across Europe, the Americas, Asia and the Middle East. He also officiates for other promotions, from Oktagon in Central Europe to UAE Warriors.

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## What Are Marc Goddard’s Most Memorable Fights?
Goddard has been in the cage for some of the biggest nights in recent UFC history.
> “At the top level, the guys are pushing themselves to the limit.”

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## What Are Marc Goddard’s Most Memorable Fights?
### Holly Holm vs Bethe Correia, UFC Singapore (2017)
Holm landed a head kick in the third round, and Correia dropped unconscious. Goddard dived in to block Holm’s follow-up punch before it landed. It’s often used as an example of a referee getting the timing exactly right.

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## What Are Marc Goddard’s Most Memorable Fights?
### Ilia Topuria vs Charles Oliveira, UFC 317 (2025)
Goddard oversaw the vacant lightweight title fight between Ilia Topuria and Charles Oliveira. Topuria won by first-round knockout, becoming a two-weight champion.

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## What Are Marc Goddard’s Most Memorable Fights?
### Justin Gaethje vs Ilia Topuria, UFC White House (2026)
In June 2026, Goddard refereed the lightweight title fight on the historic UFC White House card. Gaethje took the title when Topuria’s corner stopped the fight after the fourth round.

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## What Are Marc Goddard’s Most Memorable Fights?
### Christian Leroy Duncan vs Brendan Allen, UFC Vegas 122 (2026)
In October 2026, Goddard deducted a point from Duncan for a repeated eye poke. He later explained on X that he had warned Duncan in the first round and again before the second. He also called Duncan “a credit to the sport of MMA & an exceptional athlete.”

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## What Is Marc Goddard’s Refereeing Philosophy?
Goddard’s approach is simple: the fighters’ safety comes first, and the referee should never become the story.
He knows what fighters put into every bout, because he was one.
> “Every time they’re in there, they leave a little bit of themselves behind on that canvas.”
That is why a referee sometimes has to step in when a fighter won’t. Fighters are trained never to quit. The referee has to judge when carrying on puts them in real danger.
> “Sometimes we have to make a decision that the fighters can’t.”
He values fairness and decisiveness, and he goes by the rulebook. He has described perfection as “a journey” rather than a destination. In the end, he measures a good night the same way every time.
> “At the end of the day, all I want those two people to do is get up and walk out that cage unassisted.”

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## Why Won’t Marc Goddard Referee Certain Fighters?
Goddard steps aside from fights where people could question his neutrality. The best-known case is former UFC welterweight champion Leon Edwards. Goddard was Edwards’ first MMA coach, so he won’t referee him in the UFC.
He also asked not to referee the Israel Adesanya vs Alex Pereira rematch. He said the night belongs to the fighters.
> “We never want to be the story; I never want to be the story.”
With so many experienced referees now working with athletic commissions, he believes stepping aside is the fairest choice.

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## What Does a UFC Referee Actually Do?
A UFC referee enforces the rules of the UFC and protects both fighters from the opening bell to the final horn. The job starts well before the walkouts.
Before a fight, the referee meets each fighter in the locker room to go over the rules and answer questions. The referee checks fighters’ kit, including gloves, groin protection and mouthguards. Under the Unified Rules of MMA, every fighter must wear a mouthguard.
During the fight, the referee:
*   watches for fouls such as eye pokes, groin strikes and blows to the back of the head  
*   issues warnings and takes points away when fouls are repeated  
*   pauses the action for the doctor to check an injury  
*   stops the fight when a fighter can no longer defend themselves
For Goddard, getting it right starts with preparation.
> “If I turn up ill-prepared, something could go wrong. So my own experience, you know, it’s taught me well that I’m going to come prepared.”

**Herb Dean** (born September 30, 1970) is an American professional mixed martial artsreferee and former mixed martial artist. Dean has worked events put on by the Ultimate Fighting Championship and ONE Championship promotions, among others. He is frequently called the gold standard for referees in MMA.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-2)

## UFC and notable matches
[edit]
At UFC 48, held on June 19, 2004, Dean refereed a bout between Tim Sylvia and Frank Mir for the vacant UFC Heavyweight Championship. At 50 seconds of round one, Dean called a stop to the fight when he saw Sylvia's right forearm break due to an armbar. Due to the close proximity of a UFC cameraman, in the video footage a shocked Dean can be heard shouting "Oh, shit!" when he saw the break, and he immediately moved in to stop the fight. This proved difficult, because Sylvia, who was still trying to defend the armbar, argued with him for several seconds, despite Dean's telling him "Stop, stop, stop! The fight is over!" Once freed from the armbar, Sylvia again began to argue with Dean, who continually told him, "It's fucking broken! Your arm is broken." Sylvia protested, claiming his arm was perfectly fine and even moving it around with no apparent problems. Dean, however, insisted that "I heard it snap. I saw it go." Ringside physician Dr. Margaret Goodman agreed with Dean's assessment, and the fight was not restarted. In the post-fight interview, Sylvia again denied that his arm was broken, however the slow-motion replay showed the break happening, and an X-ray that evening showed significant damage to Sylvia's arm, which required surgery and a long recovery.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-3) Sylvia later admitted that he knew his arm was broken and wanted to keep fighting in spite of that, but he thanked Dean for saving his career by ending the fight when he did.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-4)

## UFC and notable matches
At UFC 61, held on July 8, 2006, Dean served as referee of the highly anticipated rematch between Tito Ortiz and Ken Shamrock. At 1:18 into the first round, Dean stepped in and stopped the fight following several consecutive unanswered elbows to the head of Shamrock by Ortiz, giving the victory to Ortiz by TKO. Shamrock, visibly angered, immediately protested the decision. However, it was not overturned and Shamrock was subsequently ushered out of the Octagon. A rematch was held during Ortiz vs. Shamrock 3: The Final Chapter with Ortiz once again claiming victory in a very similar fashion to the second fight, although Shamrock did not question this decision.
At UFC 70, held on April 21, 2007, Dean was the referee during the bout between Mirko Cro Cop and Gabriel Gonzaga. Late in the first round, Dean stood the fight up from the guard position, a measure typically used against inactivity. Some fight analysts claim that Gonzaga was in fact administering ground and pound and had just maneuvered his opponent against the cage for an additional advantage. Shortly after the stand up, Gonzaga knocked out Filipović with a kick to the head.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-5) Filipović collapsed awkwardly after receiving the blow, pinning his right foot, which was rotated 180 degrees backwards, underneath his body. Dean quickly freed the pinned foot which helped prevent serious injury. Filipović has stated since that the elbows on the ground confused and damaged him enough that he was disoriented after the stand up, contributing to the subsequent knockout.

## UFC and notable matches
UFC president Dana White stated after UFC 109 and UFC 160, that he thinks Dean "is one of the best referees in this business. Actually, I think he's the best" in reference to his stoppage in the fight between Mike Swick and Paulo Thiago.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-6) He added that after Dean's stoppage of the Mir vs. Sylvia fight he never questions Dean. "When Herb Dean does shit, I don't even question it anymore. I wait for the replay. This guy sees shit that I can't see sitting there watching the monitor."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-7) At UFC 169, Dean caused controversy over his stoppage of the main card fight Renan Barão vs. Urijah Faber for the UFC bantamweight title. UFC president Dana White criticized Dean saying, "He made a mistake."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-8)
At UFC Fight Night: Hunt vs. Oleinik, Dean was heavily criticized for a late stoppage during his refereeing of a fight between Khalid Murtazaliev and C. B. Dollaway. Many fans took to Twitter afterwards, with near universal criticism towards the stoppage, comparing it to a recent late stoppage by fellow referee Mario Yamasaki.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-9)
At UFC 235, Dean was criticized by UFC president Dana White after he awarded a win to Ben Askren via bulldog choke against Robbie Lawler after he thought Lawler had lost consciousness.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-10)
At UFC on ESPN: Whittaker vs. Till, Dean received more criticism for his late stoppage of a fight between Francisco Trinaldo and Jai Herbert, and got into an altercation with UFC commentator and former fighter Dan Hardy over the stoppage.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-12)

## UFC and notable matches
At UFC 229, held on October 6, 2018, Dean refereed what is considered to be one of the most anticipated fights of all time, Khabib Nurmagomedov vs Conor McGregor. # Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
October 22, 2026
When the cage door closes, two fighters and one referee are left inside. For more than 15 years, that referee has often been Marc Goddard.
Born in Birmingham, Goddard has officiated UFC world title fights before 60,000 fans. He has refereed nearly 2,000 bouts worldwide. Fighters, coaches and fans count him among the most respected officials in mixed martial arts.
> “The responsibility I carry as a referee is paramount.”
Here’s how a former West Midlands fighter became one of the UFC’s most trusted referees.
texts.9:
# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## Who Is Marc Goddard?
Marc Goddard is an English MMA referee from Birmingham. He has refereed in the UFC since 2008. Before refereeing, he was a professional fighter, coach and promoter, so he’s seen the sport from every side of the cage.
Away from fight night, Goddard is Director of Regulatory Affairs at the International Mixed Martial Arts Federation (IMMAF). He also helped found the UK safety charity Safe MMA. In 2022, he was named Referee of the Year at the Fighters Only World MMA Awards.
texts.10:
# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## How Did Marc Goddard Become an MMA Referee?
Goddard came to refereeing as a fighter. He competed as a heavyweight in the early days of the British MMA scene, finishing with a reported professional record of 7-6-1.
He got his first refereeing job by accident in 2004. A promoter’s referee didn’t show up, and Goddard stepped in. He kept fighting at the same time, and that gave him a view from both sides.
> “When I first started reffing in 2004, I was still competing. I was still fighting. So I kind of understood from that side of it.”
He learned early how seriously to take the job. Goddard has also coached fighters, including the young Leon Edwards. He still trains himself.
> “Still, being a martial artist is very important to me. From a personal point of view, I’ll never stop.”
texts.11:
# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## When Did Marc Goddard Start Refereeing in the UFC?
Goddard made his UFC debut at UFC 89 in his home city of Birmingham in 2008. Lightweight Jim Miller made his UFC debut on the same card. Goddard later marked the anniversary on social media: “We both made our debuts for the organization that night!”
Since then, he has refereed UFC events across Europe, the Americas, Asia and the Middle East. He also officiates for other promotions, from Oktagon in Central Europe to UAE Warriors.

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## What Are Marc Goddard’s Most Memorable Fights?
Goddard has been in the cage for some of the biggest nights in recent UFC history.
> “At the top level, the guys are pushing themselves to the limit.”

## What Are Marc Goddard’s Most Memorable Fights?
### Holly Holm vs Bethe Correia, UFC Singapore (2017)
Holm landed a head kick in the third round, and Correia dropped unconscious. Goddard dived in to block Holm’s follow-up punch before it landed. It’s often used as an example of a referee getting the timing exactly right.

## What Are Marc Goddard’s Most Memorable Fights?

In October 2026, Goddard deducted a point from Duncan for a repeated eye poke. He later explained on X that he had warned Duncan in the first round and again before the second. He also called Duncan “a credit to the sport of MMA & an exceptional athlete.”

# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## What Is Marc Goddard’s Refereeing Philosophy?
Goddard’s approach is simple: the fighters’ safety comes first, and the referee should never become the story.
He knows what fighters put into every bout, because he was one.
> “Every time they’re in there, they leave a little bit of themselves behind on that canvas.”
That is why a referee sometimes has to step in when a fighter won’t. Fighters are trained never to quit. The referee has to judge when carrying on puts them in real danger.
> “Sometimes we have to make a decision that the fighters can’t.”
He values fairness and decisiveness, and he goes by the rulebook. He has described perfection as “a journey” rather than a destination. In the end, he measures a good night the same way every time.
> “At the end of the day, all I want those two people to do is get up and walk out that cage unassisted.”
texts.18:
# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## Why Won’t Marc Goddard Referee Certain Fighters?
Goddard steps aside from fights where people could question his neutrality. The best-known case is former UFC welterweight champion Leon Edwards. Goddard was Edwards’ first MMA coach, so he won’t referee him in the UFC.
He also asked not to referee the Israel Adesanya vs Alex Pereira rematch. He said the night belongs to the fighters.
> “We never want to be the story; I never want to be the story.”
With so many experienced referees now working with athletic commissions, he believes stepping aside is the fairest choice.
texts.19:
# Who Is Marc Goddard? The British Referee at the Heart of the UFC
## What Does a UFC Referee Actually Do?
A UFC referee enforces the rules of the UFC and protects both fighters from the opening bell to the final horn. The job starts well before the walkouts.
Before a fight, the referee meets each fighter in the locker room to go over the rules and answer questions. The referee checks fighters’ kit, including gloves, groin protection and mouthguards. Under the Unified Rules of MMA, every fighter must wear a mouthguard.
During the fight, the referee:
*   watches for fouls such as eye pokes, groin strikes and blows to the back of the head  
*   issues warnings and takes points away when fouls are repeated  
*   pauses the action for the doctor to check an injury  
*   stops the fight when a fighter can no longer defend themselves
For Goddard, getting it right starts with preparation.
> “If I turn up ill-prepared, something could go wrong. So my own experience, you know, it’s taught me well that I’m going to come prepared.”

## UFC and notable matches
[edit]
At UFC 48, held on June 19, 2004, Dean refereed a bout between Tim Sylvia and Frank Mir for the vacant UFC Heavyweight Championship. At 50 seconds of round one, Dean called a stop to the fight when he saw Sylvia's right forearm break due to an armbar. Due to the close proximity of a UFC cameraman, in the video footage a shocked Dean can be heard shouting "Oh, shit!" when he saw the break, and he immediately moved in to stop the fight. This proved difficult, because Sylvia, who was still trying to defend the armbar, argued with him for several seconds, despite Dean's telling him "Stop, stop, stop! The fight is over!" Once freed from the armbar, Sylvia again began to argue with Dean, who continually told him, "It's fucking broken! Your arm is broken." Sylvia protested, claiming his arm was perfectly fine and even moving it around with no apparent problems. Dean, however, insisted that "I heard it snap. I saw it go." Ringside physician Dr. Margaret Goodman agreed with Dean's assessment, and the fight was not restarted. In the post-fight interview, Sylvia again denied that his arm was broken, however the slow-motion replay showed the break happening, and an X-ray that evening showed significant damage to Sylvia's arm, which required surgery and a long recovery.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-3) Sylvia later admitted that he knew his arm was broken and wanted to keep fighting in spite of that, but he thanked Dean for saving his career by ending the fight when he did.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-4)
texts.2:
## UFC and notable matches
At UFC 61, held on July 8, 2006, Dean served as referee of the highly anticipated rematch between Tito Ortiz and Ken Shamrock. At 1:18 into the first round, Dean stepped in and stopped the fight following several consecutive unanswered elbows to the head of Shamrock by Ortiz, giving the victory to Ortiz by TKO. Shamrock, visibly angered, immediately protested the decision. However, it was not overturned and Shamrock was subsequently ushered out of the Octagon. A rematch was held during Ortiz vs. Shamrock 3: The Final Chapter with Ortiz once again claiming victory in a very similar fashion to the second fight, although Shamrock did not question this decision.
At UFC 70, held on April 21, 2007, Dean was the referee during the bout between Mirko Cro Cop and Gabriel Gonzaga. Late in the first round, Dean stood the fight up from the guard position, a measure typically used against inactivity. Some fight analysts claim that Gonzaga was in fact administering ground and pound and had just maneuvered his opponent against the cage for an additional advantage. Shortly after the stand up, Gonzaga knocked out Filipović with a kick to the head.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-5) Filipović collapsed awkwardly after receiving the blow, pinning his right foot, which was rotated 180 degrees backwards, underneath his body. Dean quickly freed the pinned foot which helped prevent serious injury. Filipović has stated since that the elbows on the ground confused and damaged him enough that he was disoriented after the stand up, contributing to the subsequent knockout.

**Herb Dean** (born September 30, 1970) is an American professional mixed martial artsreferee and former mixed martial artist. Dean has worked events put on by the Ultimate Fighting Championship and ONE Championship promotions, among others. He is frequently called the gold standard for referees in MMA.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-2)

## UFC and notable matches
[edit]
At UFC 48, held on June 19, 2004, Dean refereed a bout between Tim Sylvia and Frank Mir for the vacant UFC Heavyweight Championship. At 50 seconds of round one, Dean called a stop to the fight when he saw Sylvia's right forearm break due to an armbar. Due to the close proximity of a UFC cameraman, in the video footage a shocked Dean can be heard shouting "Oh, shit!" when he saw the break, and he immediately moved in to stop the fight. This proved difficult, because Sylvia, who was still trying to defend the armbar, argued with him for several seconds, despite Dean's telling him "Stop, stop, stop! The fight is over!" Once freed from the armbar, Sylvia again began to argue with Dean, who continually told him, "It's fucking broken! Your arm is broken." Sylvia protested, claiming his arm was perfectly fine and even moving it around with no apparent problems. Dean, however, insisted that "I heard it snap. I saw it go." Ringside physician Dr. Margaret Goodman agreed with Dean's assessment, and the fight was not restarted. In the post-fight interview, Sylvia again denied that his arm was broken, however the slow-motion replay showed the break happening, and an X-ray that evening showed significant damage to Sylvia's arm, which required surgery and a long recovery.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-3) Sylvia later admitted that he knew his arm was broken and wanted to keep fighting in spite of that, but he thanked Dean for saving his career by ending the fight when he did.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-4)

## UFC and notable matches
At UFC 61, held on July 8, 2006, Dean served as referee of the highly anticipated rematch between Tito Ortiz and Ken Shamrock. At 1:18 into the first round, Dean stepped in and stopped the fight following several consecutive unanswered elbows to the head of Shamrock by Ortiz, giving the victory to Ortiz by TKO. Shamrock, visibly angered, immediately protested the decision. However, it was not overturned and Shamrock was subsequently ushered out of the Octagon. A rematch was held during Ortiz vs. Shamrock 3: The Final Chapter with Ortiz once again claiming victory in a very similar fashion to the second fight, although Shamrock did not question this decision.
At UFC 70, held on April 21, 2007, Dean was the referee during the bout between Mirko Cro Cop and Gabriel Gonzaga. Late in the first round, Dean stood the fight up from the guard position, a measure typically used against inactivity. Some fight analysts claim that Gonzaga was in fact administering ground and pound and had just maneuvered his opponent against the cage for an additional advantage. Shortly after the stand up, Gonzaga knocked out Filipović with a kick to the head.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-5) Filipović collapsed awkwardly after receiving the blow, pinning his right foot, which was rotated 180 degrees backwards, underneath his body. Dean quickly freed the pinned foot which helped prevent serious injury. Filipović has stated since that the elbows on the ground confused and damaged him enough that he was disoriented after the stand up, contributing to the subsequent knockout.

## UFC and notable matches
UFC president Dana White stated after UFC 109 and UFC 160, that he thinks Dean "is one of the best referees in this business. Actually, I think he's the best" in reference to his stoppage in the fight between Mike Swick and Paulo Thiago.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-6) He added that after Dean's stoppage of the Mir vs. Sylvia fight he never questions Dean. "When Herb Dean does shit, I don't even question it anymore. I wait for the replay. This guy sees shit that I can't see sitting there watching the monitor."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-7) At UFC 169, Dean caused controversy over his stoppage of the main card fight Renan Barão vs. Urijah Faber for the UFC bantamweight title. UFC president Dana White criticized Dean saying, "He made a mistake."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-8)
At UFC Fight Night: Hunt vs. Oleinik, Dean was heavily criticized for a late stoppage during his refereeing of a fight between Khalid Murtazaliev and C. B. Dollaway. Many fans took to Twitter afterwards, with near universal criticism towards the stoppage, comparing it to a recent late stoppage by fellow referee Mario Yamasaki.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-9)
At UFC 235, Dean was criticized by UFC president Dana White after he awarded a win to Ben Askren via bulldog choke against Robbie Lawler after he thought Lawler had lost consciousness.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-10)
At UFC on ESPN: Whittaker vs. Till, Dean received more criticism for his late stoppage of a fight between Francisco Trinaldo and Jai Herbert, and got into an altercation with UFC commentator and former fighter Dan Hardy over the stoppage.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-12)

## UFC and notable matches
At UFC 229, held on October 6, 2018, Dean refereed what is considered to be one of the most anticipated fights of all time, Khabib Nurmagomedov vs Conor McGregor. A post fight video emerged where Dean was conversing with Nurmagomedov regarding the illegal moves by McGregor not called during the match.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-13)
At UFC Freedom 250, Dean refereed the bout between Josh Hokit and Derrick Lewis, as well as the interim heavyweight championship fight between Alex Pereira and Ciryl Gane.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-14) Dean ruled the latter fight a TKO loss for Pereira in the second round. In the days after the event, Pereira argued that Gane landed several illegal strikes to the back of the head after dropping him with a legal punch, and criticized Dean for his perceived failure to intervene. Pereira claimed he spoke to Dean before the fight about the possibility of Gane committing illegal strikes, and called for Dean to "be punished" and face "legal consequences."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-15)

## UFC and notable matches

At UFC 48, held on June 19, 2004, Dean refereed a bout between Tim Sylvia and Frank Mir for the vacant UFC Heavyweight Championship. At 50 seconds of round one, Dean called a stop to the fight when he saw Sylvia's right forearm break due to an armbar. Due to the close proximity of a UFC cameraman, in the video footage a shocked Dean can be heard shouting "Oh, shit!" when he saw the break, and he immediately moved in to stop the fight. This proved difficult, because Sylvia, who was still trying to defend the armbar, argued with him for several seconds, despite Dean's telling him "Stop, stop, stop! The fight is over!" Once freed from the armbar, Sylvia again began to argue with Dean, who continually told him, "It's fucking broken! Your arm is broken." Sylvia protested, claiming his arm was perfectly fine and even moving it around with no apparent problems. Dean, however, insisted that "I heard it snap. I saw it go." Ringside physician Dr. Margaret Goodman agreed with Dean's assessment, and the fight was not restarted. In the post-fight interview, Sylvia again denied that his arm was broken, however the slow-motion replay showed the break happening, and an X-ray that evening showed significant damage to Sylvia's arm, which required surgery and a long recovery.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-3) Sylvia later admitted that he knew his arm was broken and wanted to keep fighting in spite of that, but he thanked Dean for saving his career by ending the fight when he did.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-4)
texts.2:
## UFC and notable matches
At UFC 61, held on July 8, 2006, Dean served as referee of the highly anticipated rematch between Tito Ortiz and Ken Shamrock. At 1:18 into the first round, Dean stepped in and stopped the fight following several consecutive unanswered elbows to the head of Shamrock by Ortiz, giving the victory to Ortiz by TKO. Shamrock, visibly angered, immediately protested the decision. However, it was not overturned and Shamrock was subsequently ushered out of the Octagon. A rematch was held during Ortiz vs. Shamrock 3: The Final Chapter with Ortiz once again claiming victory in a very similar fashion to the second fight, although Shamrock did not question this decision.
At UFC 70, held on April 21, 2007, Dean was the referee during the bout between Mirko Cro Cop and Gabriel Gonzaga. Late in the first round, Dean stood the fight up from the guard position, a measure typically used against inactivity. Some fight analysts claim that Gonzaga was in fact administering ground and pound and had just maneuvered his opponent against the cage for an additional advantage. Shortly after the stand up, Gonzaga knocked out Filipović with a kick to the head.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-5) Filipović collapsed awkwardly after receiving the blow, pinning his right foot, which was rotated 180 degrees backwards, underneath his body. Dean quickly freed the pinned foot which helped prevent serious injury. Filipović has stated since that the elbows on the ground confused and damaged him enough that he was disoriented after the stand up, contributing to the subsequent knockout.
texts.3:
## UFC and notable matches
UFC president Dana White stated after UFC 109 and UFC 160, that he thinks Dean "is one of the best referees in this business. Actually, I think he's the best" in reference to his stoppage in the fight between Mike Swick and Paulo Thiago.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-6) He added that after Dean's stoppage of the Mir vs. Sylvia fight he never questions Dean. "When Herb Dean does shit, I don't even question it anymore. I wait for the replay. This guy sees shit that I can't see sitting there watching the monitor."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-7) At UFC 169, Dean caused controversy over his stoppage of the main card fight Renan Barão vs. Urijah Faber for the UFC bantamweight title. UFC president Dana White criticized Dean saying, "He made a mistake."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-8)
At UFC Fight Night: Hunt vs. Oleinik, Dean was heavily criticized for a late stoppage during his refereeing of a fight between Khalid Murtazaliev and C. B. Dollaway. Many fans took to Twitter afterwards, with near universal criticism towards the stoppage, comparing it to a recent late stoppage by fellow referee Mario Yamasaki.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-9)
At UFC 235, Dean was criticized by UFC president Dana White after he awarded a win to Ben Askren via bulldog choke against Robbie Lawler after he thought Lawler had lost consciousness.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-10)
At UFC on ESPN: Whittaker vs. Till, Dean received more criticism for his late stoppage of a fight between Francisco Trinaldo and Jai Herbert, and got into an altercation with UFC commentator and former fighter Dan Hardy over the stoppage.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-12)
texts.4:
## UFC and notable matches
At UFC 229, held on October 6, 2018, Dean refereed what is considered to be one of the most anticipated fights of all time, Khabib Nurmagomedov vs Conor McGregor. A post fight video emerged where Dean was conversing with Nurmagomedov regarding the illegal moves by McGregor not called during the match.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-13)
At UFC Freedom 250, Dean refereed the bout between Josh Hokit and Derrick Lewis, as well as the interim heavyweight championship fight between Alex Pereira and Ciryl Gane.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-14) Dean ruled the latter fight a TKO loss for Pereira in the second round. In the days after the event, Pereira argued that Gane landed several illegal strikes to the back of the head after dropping him with a legal punch, and criticized Dean for his perceived failure to intervene. Pereira claimed he spoke to Dean before the fight about the possibility of Gane committing illegal strikes, and called for Dean to "be punished" and face "legal consequences."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-15)

# Dana White: Herb Dean 'did a horrible job in the 5th round' of Jones vs. Cormier
Kyle Smith• ·
When UFC president Dana White has an opinion, it's only a matter of time before everyone knows about it.
Following Saturday's thrilling Light Heavyweight title fight between Jon Jones and Daniel Cormier at UFC 182, White was critical of veteran referee Herb Dean's handling of the clinch-heavy final round.
"Herb Dean, I always talk about him; I think he's my favorite referee,"White told UFC on FOX, as relayed by MMAMania's Adam Guillen Jr. "He did a horrible job in the fifth round. He let them clinch, literally for five minutes, but other than that, it was an amazing fight."
It's unsurprising that White would call out an official. He's been quite vocal about his distaste for decisions made by referees like Dan Miragliotta and Steve Mazzagattiin the past, and was likely looking for a Jones/Cormier finish in light of the parade of decision victories that littered the main card of the UFC's first show of 2015.

**Herb Dean** (born September 30, 1970) is an American professional mixed martial artsreferee and former mixed martial artist. Dean has worked events put on by the Ultimate Fighting Championship and ONE Championship promotions, among others. He is frequently called the gold standard for referees in MMA.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Dean#cite_note-2)

## UFC and notable matches
[edit]
At UFC 48, held on June 19, 2004, Dean refereed a bout between Tim Sylvia and Frank Mir for the vacant UFC Heavyweight Championship. At 50 seconds of round one, Dean called a stop to the fight when he saw Sylvia's right forearm break due to an armbar. Due to the close proximity of a UFC cameraman, in the video footage a shocked Dean can be heard shouting "Oh, shit!" when he saw the break, and he immediately moved in to stop the fight. This proved difficult, because Sylvia, who was still trying to defend the armbar, argued with him for several seconds, despite Dean's telling him "Stop, stop, stop! The fight is over!" Once freed from the armbar, Sylvia again began to argue with Dean, who continually told him, "It's fucking broken! Your arm is broken." # Dana White criticizes referee Herb Dean’s performance in Ultimate Fighter finals fight
byChuck Mindenhall
Dec 12, 2015, 9:47 AM UTC
*
Esther Lin, Sportsfile
LAS VEGAS – With Ryan Hall winning the 22nd edition of The Ultimate Fighter by scoring a decision over Artem Lobov on Friday night, there were a few boo birds to be found.
One of them was UFC president Dana White, though he wasn't booing the fight or the performances. He was booing veteran referee Herb Dean for allowing Hall to ride on Lobov's back for a couple of minutes in the third round. And he wasn't very happy with anybody who criticized the grappling ace Hall for his efforts.
“I’ll tell you what, if any of you saw what I tweeted at the end of the night, what drove me crazy was that Herb Dean let him stay on his back for the last three minutes standing,” White said in the post-fight press conference at the Cosmopolitan. “No damage was being done. Nobody was really advancing their position. And this is for everything — this is for The Ultimate Fighter.”
White didn’t like that Dean allowed Hall to remain on Lobov’s back, which — though a dominant position — played into a stalemate for a long sequence.
“Stand them back up and...Herb I think is one of the best,” White said. “I don’t think he did his best tonight. And then I saw a lot of people talking negatively about [Hall]. One of the things about this kid is, with his jiu-jitsu, it’s so sick and at such a high level. You haven’t seen a guy who can go in and just slide in and take the leg and try to step over to the other side. You know, you’re in his guard and try to step to the other side and he gets the leg, and he goes from one thing to another to the back. And even though he didn’t get the submission, if he had pulled off one of those submissions people wouldn’t be bitching about it
“Which is one of the reasons I think that Herb should have allowed them to fight for the last three minutes. There was no fighting in the last three minutes of that fight. That’s irritating. You know, and I think that leaves a bad taste in everybody’s mouth.”

LAS VEGAS – With Ryan Hall winning the 22nd edition of The Ultimate Fighter by scoring a decision over Artem Lobov on Friday night, there were a few boo birds to be found.
One of them was UFC president Dana White, though he wasn't booing the fight or the performances. He was booing veteran referee Herb Dean for allowing Hall to ride on Lobov's back for a couple of minutes in the third round. And he wasn't very happy with anybody who criticized the grappling ace Hall for his efforts.
“I’ll tell you what, if any of you saw what I tweeted at the end of the night, what drove me crazy was that Herb Dean let him stay on his back for the last three minutes standing,” White said in the post-fight press conference at the Cosmopolitan. “No damage was being done. Nobody was really advancing their position. And this is for everything — this is for The Ultimate Fighter.”
White didn’t like that Dean allowed Hall to remain on Lobov’s back, which — though a dominant position — played into a stalemate for a long sequence.
“Stand them back up and...Herb I think is one of the best,” White said. “I don’t think he did his best tonight. And then I saw a lot of people talking negatively about [Hall]. One of the things about this kid is, with his jiu-jitsu, it’s so sick and at such a high level. You haven’t seen a guy who can go in and just slide in and take the leg and try to step over to the other side. You know, you’re in his guard and try to step to the other side and he gets the leg, and he goes from one thing to another to the back. And even though he didn’t get the submission, if he had pulled off one of those submissions people wouldn’t be bitching about it
“Which is one of the reasons I think that Herb should have allowed them to fight for the last three minutes. There was no fighting in the last three minutes of that fight. That’s irritating. You know, and I think that leaves a bad taste in everybody’s mouth.”
